title: Save a player as bytes
description:
Writing a struct to a file as raw memory would include its padding (leftover bytes) and depend on the compiler's layout. Save files are written member by member instead, in a fixed format.

Write `savePlayer(p)`, which returns the bytes of a `Player` in this exact format, with no padding, all numbers little-endian:

| Bytes | Field |
|---|---|
| 0 to 3 | `id`, a `std::uint32_t` |
| 4 to 5 | `health`, a `std::int16_t` |
| 6 | `level`, a `std::uint8_t` |
| 7 to 10 | `gold`, a `std::uint32_t` |

So every saved player is exactly 11 bytes, even though `sizeof(Player)` is 12. Then write `loadPlayer(bytes)`, which reads the same format back.
hints: A helper that appends the lowest `n` bytes of a number, lowest first, does most of the saving: `value >> (8 * i)` brings byte `i` down to the bottom, and converting to `std::uint8_t` keeps only that byte.
Loading is the reverse: start from 0 and OR in each byte shifted left by `8 * i`.
For the signed `health`, convert to `std::uint16_t` first when saving, and back through `std::uint16_t` to `std::int16_t` when loading. The bits are the same; only their meaning changes.
rules: Write each field byte by byte, so the format does not depend on the compiler's layout or padding.
lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out
